items.stem: Hold your breath for as long as you can and then breathe out slowly. Question : (i) How long can you hold your breath? (ii) How do you feel when you hold your breath?
items.answer: (i) This is different for everyone! Some people can hold their breath for a shorter time, maybe less than half a minute, while others might hold it for closer to a minute or even more. You have to try it and see how long you can hold it comfortably. There isn’t one single correct time. (ii) When you hold your breath : Your body keeps using the oxygen (the gas we need from the air) that you last breathed in. At the same time, your body keeps making a waste gas called carbon dioxide. items.answer: (i) [ T ] (ii) [ F ] – Machines are man-made resources. (iii) [ T ] (iv) [ T ]

items.stem: Classify the following as renewable or non- renewable resources—coal, natural gas, forests and minerals.
items.answer: Renewable : Forests Non-renewable : Coal, Natural gas, Minerals

items.stem: Why do we say that petroleum is a non-renewable resource?
items.answer: Petroleum forms very slowly over millions of years from dead plants and animals buried deep in the Earth. Because we use it much faster than it is created, it cannot be replaced within a human lifetime, so it is called non-renewable.

items.stem: It is difficult to regrow forests. Justify this statement.
items.answer: Trees take many years to mature, and a forest includes layers of plants, soil organisms and wildlife that develop together. After large-scale cutting, soil erodes, seeds dry up and the climate changes, so bringing back the same rich forest is slow and difficult.

items.stem: What is the primary purpose of windmills ?

options.label: A
options.text: To provide shade in sunny areas

options.label: B
options.text: To create artificial wind for cooling

options.label: C
options.text: To run flour mills, pull up water, or generate electricity using wind energy

options.label: D
options.text: To act as decorative structures in farms

items.answer: (C) To run flour mills, pull up water, or generate electricity using wind energy. Windmills harness the energy of the wind to perform useful work, such as grinding grain in flour mills, pumping water from wells, or, most commonly in modern times, generating electricity.

items.stem: What is saline water?

options.label: A
options.text: Water that is fresh and suitable for drinking

options.label: B
options.text: Water that is found in glaciers and ice sheets

options.label: C
options.text: Water that is salty, like the water found in oceans and seas

options.label: D
options.text: Water that has been purified through filtration

items.answer: (C) Water that is salty, like the water found in oceans and seas. Saline water is characterized by its high salt content. The vast majority of Earth’s water, found in oceans and seas, is saline and not directly suitable for drinking or most agricultural uses.

items.stem: What proportion of the Earth’s surface is covered by water?

options.label: A
options.text: About one-third

options.label: B
options.text: About half

options.label: C
options.text: About two-thirds

options.label: D
options.text: About three-fourths

items.answer: (C) About two-thirds The water covers approximately two-thirds of the Earth’s surface, with most of this water being saline and found in oceans and seas.

items.stem: What is the main difference between saline water and freshwater in terms of usability for domestic purposes?

options.label: A
options.text: Saline water is always hotter than freshwater

options.label: B
options.text: Freshwater is salty, while saline water is not

options.label: C
options.text: Saline water is not fit for domestic use due to its salt content; freshwater is suitable

options.label: D
options.text: Freshwater can only be found underground

items.answer: (C) Saline water is not fit for domestic use due to its salt content; freshwater is suitable. The high salt concentration in saline water makes it unsuitable for drinking, agriculture, and most industrial uses without desalination. Freshwater has a low salt content and is essential for these activities.

items.stem: Which of the following activities leads to water pollution, as mentioned in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Rainwater harvesting

options.label: B
options.text: Dumping waste from homes and industries into water sources

options.label: C
options.text: Using water efficiently for hand washing

options.label: D
options.text: Performing breathing exercises near a river

items.answer: (B) Dumping waste from homes and industries into water sources. The chapter explicitly states that freshwater sources are polluted by throwing trash and dumping waste from homes and industries into them, rendering the water unfit for consumption.

items.stem: What is the primary purpose of rainwater harvesting?

options.label: A
options.text: To prevent floods during heavy rainfall

options.label: B
options.text: To collect and store rainwater for later use, thereby conserving water

options.label: C
options.text: To increase the salinity of groundwater

options.label: D
options.text: To generate electricity from rainwater

items.answer: (B) To collect and store rainwater for later use, thereby conserving water. Rainwater harvesting is a method of collecting and storing rainwater that falls on rooftops or other surfaces, rather than letting it run off. This stored water can then be used later, helping to conserve freshwater resources.

items.stem: There is an increasing demand of trees for industries and housing. Therefore, trees are being felled. Is it justified? Discuss and prepare a brief report.
items.answer: Cutting trees faster than they grow is not justified because it destroys habitats, causes soil erosion and raises carbon-dioxide levels. Industries should adopt sustainable practices—use recycled wood, plant two trees for every one cut and switch to alternative materials where possible. Housing projects must leave green belts and protect old trees. Communities, government and companies should work together for balanced development.

items.stem: Propose a plan to use less water in your school. What steps would you take to make this plan happen and how would it help the environment?
items.answer: Plan : Save Every Drop (i) Fix leaks : Check taps and pipes weekly; repair drips. (ii) Install push or sensor taps : They shut automatically. (iii) Reuse water : Collect wash-basin water for gardening. (iv) Awareness posters : Remind students to close taps. (v) Rain-water harvesting : Channel roof water into a storage tank. Benefits : Reduces the school’s water bill, saves groundwater, and teaches students good conservation habits, helping the environment by lowering strain on local water sources.

items.stem: What are natural resources as described in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Resources created by human beings for their convenience

options.label: B
options.text: Resources provided by nature that are essential for sustaining life

options.label: C
options.text: Only the resources found deep within the Earth, like minerals

options.label: D
options.text: Resources that are unlimited and can never be exhausted

items.answer: (B) Resources provided by nature that are essential for sustaining life. Natural resources are those materials and energy sources that are provided by nature and are vital for the survival and well-being of all life forms on Earth, including humans.

items.stem: What is the approximate percentage of oxygen in the air?
items.answer: (B) 21% The composition of air, shows that oxygen constitutes approximately 21% of the air we breathe.

items.stem: Why is air considered essential for the survival of most living beings?

options.label: A
options.text: Because it helps in keeping the weather cool

options.label: B
options.text: Because it contains oxygen, which is needed for bodily functions

options.label: C
options.text: Because it allows birds to fly easily

options.label: D
options.text: Because it is necessary for making sounds travel

items.answer: (B) Because it contains oxygen, which is needed for bodily functions. Air contains oxygen, a gas that most living organisms require for respiration. Respiration is the process that releases energy from food to perform various life functions, making oxygen vital for survival.

items.stem: What is wind?

options.label: A
options.text: Air that is very cold

options.label: B
options.text: Air that contains a lot of moisture

options.label: C
options.text: Moving air

options.label: D
options.text: Air that is found at high altitudes

items.answer: (C) Moving air. Wind as air that is in motion. This movement can range from a gentle breeze to a strong storm.

items.stem: List four activities that are possible due to the presence of air.
items.answer: Breathing, flying kites or aeroplanes, burning fuels (oxygen supports fire), running windmills to generate electricity.

items.stem: How can you contribute towards enhancing the green cover of your locality? Make a list of actions to be taken.
items.answer: 1. Plant and look after saplings along roads and in parks.

items.stem: In the given illustration, we see that food is being cooked. Answer the following questions (i) What type of energy is being used for cooking? (ii) Name one benefit and one drawback of using this type of energy for cooking.
items.answer: (i) Type of energy used : Solar energy (solar cooker). (ii) One benefit : Clean, free and renewable—no smoke or fuel cost.

items.stem: Cutting down trees on a large scale impacts the quality of the soil. Why do you think it is so?
items.answer: Tree roots bind the soil. When trees are removed the soil becomes loose and is easily washed or blown away, leading to erosion and loss of nutrients.

items.stem: Explain two ways in which human activities pollute the air. Propose one action which can help in reducing air pollution.
items.answer: 1. Vehicle exhaust : Burning petrol and diesel releases smoke and gases.

items.stem: A family uses solar panels, a gas stove and a windmill. What would happen if there were no sunlight for a week?
items.answer: The solar panels would stop producing electricity, so any appliances depending on solar power would not run. The gas stove (LPG) and the windmill would still work, but the family would face a shortage of solar electricity.

items.stem: Fill up the blanks using the following terms— fossil fuels, forest, air, petroleum, coal, water and non-renewable resource Ans :
items.answer: (B) Traditional water harvesting structures like step wells. Bawadis and Vavs are traditional stepwells found in India, particularly in arid regions. They are unique architectural structures designed for harvesting and storing rainwater and seepage water.

items.stem: What is the main source of energy on Earth, according to Ajji ?

options.label: A
options.text: Wind

options.label: B
options.text: Water

options.label: C
options.text: The Sun

options.label: D
options.text: Fossil fuels

items.answer: (C) The Sun Ajji explains, and the chapter reiterates, that the Sun is the primary source of energy for Earth. It provides heat and light essential for various processes and for sustaining life.

items.stem: How is the Sun indirectly the source of energy for a cow grazing on grass?

options.label: A
options.text: The cow directly absorbs sunlight for energy

options.label: B
options.text: The grass uses sunlight to prepare its food (photosynthesis), which the cow then eats

options.label: C
options.text: The Sun warms the ground, making the grass grow faster

options.label: D
options.text: The cow gets energy from drinking water heated by the Sun

items.answer: (B) The grass uses sunlight to prepare its food (photosynthesis), which the cow then eats. Plants like grass use solar energy to produce their own food through photosynthesis. Herbivores like cows consume these plants, thereby deriving energy that originally came from the Sun.

items.stem: A household installs panels on its rooftop that capture the Sun’s energy to produce electricity. These panels are known as:

options.label: A
options.text: Wind turbines

options.label: B
options.text: Geothermal collectors

options.label: C
options.text: Solar panels

options.label: D
options.text: Hydroelectric generators

items.answer: (C) Solar panels Solar panels are devices specifically designed to absorb sunlight and convert it into electricity (photovoltaic effect) or to heat water (solar thermal collectors). Their placement on rooftops is common for maximizing sun exposure.

items.stem: What are forests, as defined by Ajji in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Small gardens with a few trees

options.label: B
options.text: Areas cleared for farming

options.label: C
options.text: Large areas with dense growth of various types of plants

options.label: D
options.text: Places where only wild animals live, without any plants

items.answer: (C) Large areas with dense growth of various types of plants. Ajji describes forests as extensive areas characterized by a high density and variety of plant life, including trees, shrubs and herbs.

items.stem: What is Van Mahotsav?

options.label: A
options.text: A festival celebrating the harvest season

options.label: B
options.text: A week-long event in July for planting new trees and raising awareness about forests

options.label: C
options.text: A traditional method of collecting forest produce

options.label: D
options.text: A scientific study of forest ecosystems

items.answer: (B) A week-long event in July for planting new trees and raising awareness about forests. Van Mahotsav is a forest festival celebrated in India, typically in July, where new saplings are planted, and efforts are made to increase awareness about the importance of conserving forests.

items.stem: How do the roots of plants in a forest contribute to the soil?

options.label: A
options.text: They extract all nutrients, making the soil infertile

options.label: B
options.text: They hold on to the soil and prevent it from being washed away (erosion)

options.label: C
options.text: They make the soil very loose and dry

options.label: D
options.text: They convert soil directly into rock

items.answer: (B) They hold on to the soil and prevent it from being washed away (erosion). The extensive root systems of plants, especially trees in a forest, bind the soil particles together. This helps to stabilize the soil and prevent it from being eroded by wind or water.

items.stem: How is soil primarily formed?

options.label: A
options.text: By the rapid cooling of lava from volcanoes

options.label: B
options.text: By the accumulation of plastic waste over many years

options.label: C
options.text: By the disintegration (breaking apart) of rocks by actions of the Sun, water, and living organisms over a long time

options.label: D
options.text: By human activities like construction and farming

items.answer: (C) By the disintegration (breaking apart) of rocks by actions of the Sun, water, and living organisms over a long time. Soil formation is a slow, long-term process involving the weathering and breakdown of rocks due to various physical, chemical, and biological factors, including the action of sunlight, water, and organisms.

items.stem: Which of these are examples of fossil fuels mentioned in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Wood, charcoal, and cow dung

options.label: B
options.text: Sunlight, wind, and water

options.label: C
options.text: Petroleum, natural gas, and coal

options.label: D
options.text: Iron, gold, and copper

items.answer: (C) Petroleum, natural gas, and coal. Petroleum (from which petrol and diesel are derived), natural gas and coal as the commonly known fossil fuels.

items.stem: Why are petroleum, natural gas, and coal called fossil fuels?

options.label: A
options.text: Because they are found near ancient fossils of large animals

options.label: B
options.text: Because they are formed from the remains of ancient microorganisms and plants buried deep inside the Earth over millions of years

options.label: C
options.text: Because they look like fossils when extracted

options.label: D
options.text: Because they were first discovered by archaeologists studying fossils

items.answer: (B) Because they are formed from the remains of ancient microorganisms and plants buried deep inside the Earth over millions of years. Fossil fuels originate from the organic matter of prehistoric organisms (plants and tiny marine life) that were buried and subjected to intense heat and pressure over geological time scales, transforming them into these energy-rich substances.

items.stem: What are renewable resources?

options.label: A
options.text: Resources that are created by humans in factories

options.label: B
options.text: Resources that are found in unlimited quantities and will never run out

options.label: C
options.text: Resources which get renewed, replenished, or restored within a reasonable period of time through natural processes

options.label: D
options.text: Resources that can only be used once and then are gone forever

items.answer: (C) Resources which get renewed, replenished, or restored within a reasonable period of time through natural processes. Renewable resources are those that can be naturally regenerated or replenished over a relatively short time scale (within a human lifetime or so), making them sustainable if used responsibly. Air and water are examples.

items.stem: What is the main difference between renewable and non-renewable resources?

options.label: A
options.text: Renewable resources are man-made; non- renewable are natural

options.label: B
options.text: Renewable resources get replenished in a reasonable time; non-renewable resources do not or take millions of years

options.label: C
options.text: Renewable resources are always solids; non- renewable are always liquids or gases

options.label: D
options.text: Renewable resources cause pollution; non- renewable resources are clean

items.answer: (B) Renewable resources get replenished in a reasonable time; non-renewable resources do not or take millions of years. The key distinction lies in their rate of regeneration. Renewable resources (like solar energy, wind, forests if managed well) can be replenished naturally. Non-renewable resources (like fossil fuels, minerals) form over geological time scales and are finite.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of a non- renewable natural resource?

options.label: A
options.text: Air

options.label: B
options.text: Water

options.label: C
options.text: Coal

options.label: D
options.text: Forests (when sustain ably managed)

items.answer: (C) Coal Coal is a fossil fuel that formed over millions of years from ancient plant matter. It is extracted from the Earth and is found in limited quantities, making it a non-renewable resource.

items.stem: Which of the following actions helps in conserving fossil fuels?

options.label: A
options.text: Driving alone in a car for short distances

options.label: B
options.text: Using public transport or cycling instead of private vehicles

options.label: C
options.text: Leaving lights and appliances on when not in use

options.label: D
options.text: Preferring goods transported over very long distances

items.answer: (B) Using public transport or cycling instead of private vehicles. Using public transport, walking, or cycling reduces the number of individual vehicles on the road, thereby decreasing the overall consumption of fossil fuels like petrol and diesel.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : The Sun is considered the main source of energy on Earth. Reason (R) : Plants use solar energy to produce food, and animals obtain energy by eating plants or other animals that ate plants.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The Sun’s energy is captured by plants through photosynthesis. This energy then flows through the food chain as animals consume plants or other animals, making the Sun the ultimate source of energy for most life on Earth.

items.stem: A community decides to collect rainwater from rooftops and store it in large tanks for use during dry seasons. This practice is an example of:

options.label: A
options.text: Water pollution

options.label: B
options.text: Rainwater harvesting

options.label: C
options.text: Fossil fuel conservation

options.label: D
options.text: Soil erosion prevention

items.answer: (B) Rainwater harvesting Collecting and storing rainwater from rooftops or other surfaces for later use is known as rainwater harvesting. It is a method of water conservation.

items.stem: What is CNG, mentioned as a cleaner fuel for vehicles?

options.label: A
options.text: Condensed Natural Gas

options.label: B
options.text: Carbonated Natural Gas

options.label: C
options.text: Compressed Natural Gas

options.label: D
options.text: Cooled Nitrogen Gas

items.answer: (C) Compressed Natural Gas CNG stands for Compressed Natural Gas. It is used as a vehicular fuel and is generally considered cleaner burning than petrol or diesel, producing fewer pollutants.

items.stem: Why is it important to use natural resources judiciously and responsibly?

options.label: A
options.text: Because they are too expensive to extract

options.label: B
options.text: To fulfill present needs while saving for the future and without harming the environment

options.label: C
options.text: Because natural resources are only meant for human use

options.label: D
options.text: To prevent them from becoming too abundant

items.answer: (B) To fulfill present needs while saving for the future and without harming the environment. Judicious and responsible use of natural resources ensures their availability for future generations (sustainability) and minimizes negative environmental impacts associated with their over- extraction or misuse.

items.stem: What is the term for the breaking apart of rocks over a long time due to actions of the Sun, water, and living organisms?

options.label: A
options.text: Fossilization

options.label: B
options.text: Disintegration (or Weathering)

options.label: C
options.text: Sedimentation

options.label: D
options.text: Compaction

items.answer: (B) Disintegration (or Weathering) The process by which rocks are broken down into smaller pieces by physical, chemical, or biological means (like temperature changes, water action, plant roots) is called weathering or disintegration, leading to soil formation.

items.stem: Which of these metals are extracted from minerals, as mentioned in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Plastic and rubber

options.label: B
options.text: Wood and paper

options.label: C
options.text: Aluminium, gold, copper, and iron

options.label: D
options.text: Cotton and silk

items.answer: (C) Aluminium, gold, copper, and iron The chapter states that important metals such as aluminium, gold, copper, and iron are obtained by extracting them from their respective mineral ores.

items.stem: What is a key difference between air in Ajji’s village on the edge of a forest and the air in the city, as noticed by Bhoomi and Surya?

options.label: A
options.text: City air is always colder and fresher

options.label: B
options.text: Village air is fresh and cooler; city air smells of smoke and is polluted

options.label: C
options.text: Village air has more dust; city air is very clean

options.label: D
options.text: Both village and city air have identical composition and smell

items.answer: (B) Village air is fresh and cooler; city air smells of smoke and is polluted. Bhoomi and Surya observe that the air in Ajji’s village is pure, refreshing, and cooler compared to the city air, which is polluted and smells of vehicle smoke.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a use of windmills mentioned in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: To run flour mills

options.label: B
options.text: To pull up water from a well

options.label: C
options.text: To generate electricity

options.label: D
options.text: To create building materials

items.answer: (D) To create building materials. The chapter lists running flour mills, pumping water, and generating electricity as common uses of windmills. They are not typically used for creating building materials.

items.stem: If a country has many windmill farms, what natural resource is it primarily utilizing to generate power?

options.label: A
options.text: Solar energy

options.label: B
options.text: Geothermal energy

options.label: C
options.text: Wind energy

options.label: D
options.text: Fossil fuels

items.answer: (C) Wind energy Windmill farms consist of numerous windmills (wind turbines) that capture the kinetic energy of the wind and convert it into electricity.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Forests are important natural resources. Reason (R) : Forests provide food and shelter to many wild animals, prevent soil erosion, and supply various products useful to humans.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Forests are vital natural resources due to their numerous ecological and economic benefits, including supporting biodiversity, conserving soil, and providing timber, medicinal plants, and other products.

items.stem: To reduce reliance on fossil fuels for transportation, a city introduces electric vehicles that run on batteries charged using electricity. This shift primarily promotes the use of:

options.label: A
options.text: More non-renewable resources

options.label: B
options.text: Renewable energy sources

options.label: C
options.text: Geothermal energy only

options.label: D
options.text: Nuclear energy

items.answer: (B) Renewable energy sources. Electric vehicles themselves do not burn fossil fuels directly. If the electricity used to charge them comes from renewable sources like solar and wind, this represents a shift towards cleaner, sustainable energy.

items.stem: What is the composition of nitrogen in the air by percentage, according to Figure.
items.answer: (C) 78% Figure, depicting air composition, clearly shows that nitrogen makes up the largest portion of air, approximately 78%.

items.stem: Why is it mentioned that it takes many years to grow a new forest or restore lost forests?

options.label: A
options.text: Because trees only grow in specific seasons

options.label: B
options.text: Because tree seeds are very rare and difficult to find

options.label: C
options.text: Because trees are slow-growing organisms, and forest ecosystems are complex and take time to establish

options.label: D
options.text: Because animals constantly eat young saplings

items.answer: (C) Because trees are slow-growing organisms, and forest ecosystems are complex and take time to establish. Trees, especially large ones that form the backbone of a forest, grow slowly over decades or even centuries. Furthermore, a forest is a complex ecosystem involving many interdependent species, and its regeneration is a lengthy process.

items.stem: What is the general term for resources that are found in limited quantities and, once used, get exhausted because they are not produced or replenished within a reasonable period?

options.label: A
options.text: Human-made resources

options.label: B
options.text: Abundant resources

options.label: C
options.text: Renewable resources

options.label: D
options.text: Non-renewable resources

items.answer: (D) Non-renewable resources Non-renewable resources are finite and take exceptionally long periods (often millions of years) to form. Their rate of consumption far exceeds their rate of natural replenishment, leading to their eventual depletion.

items.stem: Which important weather parameter, monitored at weather stations worldwide, is mentioned as being useful for making weather forecasts?

options.label: A
options.text: Soil moisture content

options.label: B
options.text: Air temperature

options.label: C
options.text: The number of birds in an area

options.label: D
options.text: The height of the tallest trees

items.answer: (B) Air temperature Air temperature is an important weather parameter. Data gathered on air temperature, along with other parameters, is crucial for making weather forecasts.

items.stem: Why are electric vehicles mentioned as a less polluting alternative to vehicles that use fossil fuels?

options.label: A
options.text: Electric vehicles are much lighter in weight

options.label: B
options.text: Electric vehicles do not release smoke directly from their operation

options.label: C
options.text: Electric vehicles can travel much longer distances on a single charge

options.label: D
options.text: Electric vehicles are made from recycled materials

items.answer: (B) Electric vehicles do not release smoke directly from their operation. Vehicles running on fossil fuels (petrol, diesel) produce exhaust smoke containing pollutants. Electric vehicles, powered by batteries, do not have tailpipe emissions of smoke, contributing to reduced local air pollution.

items.stem: What are human-made resources?

options.label: A
options.text: Natural resources that have been slightly modified by humans

options.label: B
options.text: All resources found on Earth, including natural ones

options.label: C
options.text: Resources created by human beings for their convenience and to meet their needs

options.label: D
options.text: Resources that are only used by humans and not by other living beings

items.answer: (C) Resources created by human beings for their convenience and to meet their needs. Human-made resources are those that are developed or manufactured by humans using natural resources and technology to serve various purposes and make life more comfortable, such as buildings, tools and vehicles.

items.stem: Which of the following was NOT mentioned by Ajji as one of the treasures of nature at her village?

options.label: A
options.text: Pure air

options.label: B
options.text: Fertile soil

options.label: C
options.text: Abundant sunlight

options.label: D
options.text: Advanced communication networks

items.answer: (D) Advanced communication networks Ajji highlighted pure air, fertile soil, and abundant sunlight as some of the natural treasures of her village. Advanced communication networks are human-made infrastructure, not direct treasures of nature in this context.

items.stem: How does the availability of freshwater compare to the total amount of water on Earth’s surface?

options.label: A
options.text: Most of the Earth’s water is freshwater

options.label: B
options.text: Freshwater and saline water are found in equal proportions

options.label: C
options.text: A very small fraction of Earth’s water is easily accessible freshwater; most is saline

options.label: D
options.text: All water on Earth’s surface is freshwater

items.answer: (C) A very small fraction of Earth’s water is easily accessible freshwater; most is saline. While water covers about two-thirds of the Earth, the vast majority is saline ocean water. Easily accessible freshwater (in rivers, lakes, accessible groundwater) constitutes only a very small percentage of the total.

items.stem: All of the following are listed as uses of water in daily life or industry EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Drinking and cooking

options.label: B
options.text: Generating wind energy

options.label: C
options.text: Growing crops (agriculture)

options.label: D
options.text: Industrial processes

items.answer: (B) Generating wind energy Water is essential for drinking, cooking, bathing, agriculture, and various industrial activities. Wind energy is generated from moving air, not directly from water in the same context as the other uses.

items.stem: If a family installs a solar water heater on their roof, which natural resource are they primarily utilizing to heat their water?

options.label: A
options.text: Geothermal energy from the Earth

options.label: B
options.text: Energy from the Sun

options.label: C
options.text: Wind energy

options.label: D
options.text: Energy from burning fossil fuels

items.answer: (B) Energy from the Sun A solar water heater is designed to absorb solar radiation (sunlight) and use that energy to heat water, thus directly utilizing energy from the Sun.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Burning fossil fuels contributes to air pollution. Reason (R) : When fossil fuels are burnt, smoke and gases like carbon dioxide are produced and released into the atmosphere.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The combustion of fossil fuels releases various substances into the air, including smoke (particulate matter) and greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide, which are major contributors to air pollution.

items.stem: A village community notices that their local river is becoming dirty due to trash being thrown into it and untreated waste from a nearby small factory. This situation is an example of:

options.label: A
options.text: Efficient water management

options.label: B
options.text: Water pollution

options.label: C
options.text: Rainwater harvesting

options.label: D
options.text: Soil conservation

items.answer: (B) Water pollution. The introduction of harmful substances like trash and untreated industrial waste into the river, making it unsafe for use and harmful to aquatic life, is a clear instance of water pollution.

items.stem: What traditional practice involves digging trenches lined with stone blocks to store rainwater and seepage from nearby water bodies, common in Rajasthan and Gujarat?

options.label: A
options.text: Building large dams

options.label: B
options.text: Constructing step wells (Bawadi/Vav)

options.label: C
options.text: Using modern filtration plants

options.label: D
options.text: Covering ponds to prevent evaporation

items.answer: (B) Constructing step wells (Bawadi/Vav) The chapter describes step wells (Bawadi or Vav) as traditional water harvesting structures designed to collect and store rainwater and water seeping from other sources, especially in arid regions.

items.stem: How do earthworms contribute positively to soil health, as mentioned in the context of Ajji’s garden?

options.label: A
options.text: They compact the soil, making it harder

options.label: B
options.text: They consume all the nutrients from the soil

options.label: C
options.text: They help in turning and loosening the soil, improving aeration

options.label: D
options.text: They primarily help in spreading plant seeds

items.answer: (C) They help in turning and loosening the soil, improving aeration. Earthworms are natural agents that burrow through the soil. Their movement helps to turn over soil layers and create channels, which loosens the soil and improves air circulation within it.

items.stem: What are rocks primarily made up of?

options.label: A
options.text: Fossil fuels

options.label: B
options.text: Compressed plants

options.label: C
options.text: Minerals

options.label: D
options.text: Solidified water

items.answer: (C) Minerals Rocks are naturally occurring solid aggregates composed of one or more minerals or mineralized. Minerals are the fundamental building blocks of rocks.

items.stem: Which important event related to forest conservation is celebrated for a week across India during July, involving planting new trees?

options.label: A
options.text: Earth Day

options.label: B
options.text: World Water Day

options.label: C
options.text: Van Mahotsav

options.label: D
options.text: Wildlife Week

items.answer: (C) Van Mahotsav Van Mahotsav is described as a week-long festival in July dedicated to planting trees and promoting forest conservation and awareness across India.

items.stem: How do the consequences of over-dependence on fossil fuels differ from utilizing solar energy?

options.label: A
options.text: Fossil fuels are cleaner; solar energy causes more air pollution

options.label: B
options.text: Fossil fuels are renewable; solar energy is non- renewable

options.label: C
options.text: Burning fossil fuels causes air pollution; solar energy is a cleaner, renewable source

options.label: D
options.text: Both have identical environmental impacts

items.answer: (C) Burning fossil fuels causes air pollution; solar energy is a cleaner, renewable source. The combustion of fossil fuels is a major source of air pollution. Solar energy, being a renewable resource, is harnessed without direct emissions, making it a much cleaner alternative.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a direct use of solar energy mentioned in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Plants making food (photosynthesis)

options.label: B
options.text: Drying clothes or chillies

options.label: C
options.text: Generating electricity using solar panels

options.label: D
options.text: Powering wind turbines

items.answer: (D) Powering wind turbines. Plants use solar energy for photosynthesis, and humans use it for drying and generating electricity via solar panels. Wind turbines are powered by wind, which is indirectly influenced by solar energy (due to differential heating of Earth’s surface), but it’s not a direct use of solar energy in the same way.

items.stem: If you observe that the leaves falling from trees in a forest decay and enrich the soil, what natural process is this an example of?

options.label: A
options.text: Soil erosion

options.label: B
options.text: Water pollution

options.label: C
options.text: Recycling in nature

options.label: D
options.text: Fossil fuel formation

items.answer: (C) Recycling in nature The decomposition of fallen leaves returns nutrients to the soil, which are then used by new plants to grow. This continuous breakdown and reuse of organic matter is a fundamental part of nutrient cycling or recycling in natural ecosystems.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : It is important to conserve minerals and use them responsibly. Reason (R) : Minerals take thousands to millions of years to form and are non-renewable resources.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Minerals are formed through slow geological processes, making them non-renewable on human time scales. Their finite nature necessitates responsible use and conservation to ensure future availability.

items.stem: What gas present in the air is essential for our body to perform its functions?
items.answer: Oxygen is essential for our body to perform its functions.

items.stem: What is moving air called?
items.answer: Moving air is called wind.

items.stem: Name one use of windmills.
items.answer: Windmills can be used to generate electricity (or run flour mills, pull up water).

items.stem: What percentage of the air is composed of nitrogen?
items.answer: Nitrogen comprises approximately 78% of the air.

items.stem: What type of water is found in oceans and seas, making it unfit for most domestic uses?
items.answer: Saline or salty water is found in oceans and seas.

items.stem: Name one easily accessible source of freshwater.
items.answer: Rivers (or lakes, ponds, wells).

items.stem: What is the practice of collecting and storing rainwater for later use called?
items.answer: This practice is called rainwater harvesting.

items.stem: What is the common name for step wells in Rajasthan?
items.answer: Step wells are commonly known as Bawadi in Rajasthan.

items.stem: What is the main source of energy on Earth?
items.answer: The Sun is the main source of energy on Earth.

items.stem: What device captures the Sun’s energy to produce electricity?
items.answer: Solar panels capture the Sun’s energy to produce electricity.

items.stem: What are large areas with dense growth of various types of plants called?
items.answer: These are called forests.

items.stem: What is the week-long event celebrated in July to increase green cover called?
items.answer: This event is called Van Mahotsav.

items.stem: Name the famous movement started in the early 1970 s in Uttarakhand to prevent the cutting of trees.
items.answer: The famous movement is the Chipko movement.

items.stem: How is soil primarily formed?
items.answer: Soil is formed by the disintegration (breaking apart) of rocks.

items.stem: Name one important metal extracted from minerals found in rocks.
items.answer: Aluminium (or gold, copper, iron).

items.stem: Name one common fossil fuel obtained from petroleum.
items.answer: Petrol (or diesel, kerosene).

items.stem: What cleaner fuel, derived from natural gas, is used in vehicles?
items.answer: Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) is used.

items.stem: What are resources provided by nature called?
items.answer: Resources provided by nature are called natural resources.

items.stem: What are resources that get renewed or replenished within a reasonable period of time called?
items.answer: These are called renewable resources.

items.stem: Give one example of a non-renewable natural resource.
items.answer: Coal (or petroleum, natural gas, minerals, rocks, soil).

items.stem: List the two major gases in the air and their approximate percentages.
items.answer: The two major gases are Nitrogen (approximately 78%) and Oxygen (approximately 21%). These gases make up most of the air we breathe.

items.stem: How does a firki (paper pinwheel) demonstrate the presence of wind?
items.answer: A firki rotates when you run with it or when air blows on it. This rotation is caused by moving air, which is wind.

items.stem: Why is most of the Earth’s water not directly usable for drinking or agriculture?
items.answer: Most of the Earth’s water is found in oceans and seas, which is saline (salty) and therefore not fit for most domestic, agricultural, or industrial uses without treatment.

items.stem: What is rainwater harvesting? Give one traditional example from India.
items.answer: Rainwater harvesting is the collection and storage of rainwater for later use. A traditional example is step wells (Bawadis/Vavs) used in regions like Rajasthan and Gujarat.

items.stem: How do plants utilize energy from the Sun?
items.answer: Plants use sunlight (solar energy) to prepare their own food through the process of photosynthesis. This food supports their growth and development.

items.stem: Briefly explain how the Sun is the ultimate source of energy for a cow eating grass.
items.answer: Grass (a plant) makes its food using sunlight. The cow eats the grass, thereby obtaining energy that originally came from the Sun.

items.stem: What is a forest? Mention two important things forests provide to wild animals.
items.answer: A forest is a large area with dense growth of various plants. Forests provide food and shelter to many wild animals, including birds and insects.

items.stem: What was the Chipko movement, and what was its main aim?
items.answer: The Chipko movement, started in the 1970s in Uttarakhand, was an effort by local people, especially women, to prevent the cutting of trees by hugging them.

items.stem: How do the roots of plants and decaying leaves contribute to soil health in forests?
items.answer: Plant roots hold the soil, preventing erosion. Leaves that fall and decay enrich the soil with nutrients, supporting new plant growth.

items.stem: How are rocks used in construction? Give two examples of rocks used as building materials.
items.answer: Rocks are used for houses, buildings, roads, and dams. Slate is used for roofing, and laterite can be used as bricks.

items.stem: What are fossil fuels? Name the three main types of fossil fuels.
items.answer: Fossil fuels are formed from the ancient remains of organisms buried deep inside the Earth over millions of years. The three main types are coal, petroleum, and natural gas.

items.stem: Why is Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) considered a cleaner fuel than petrol or diesel?
items.answer: CNG is considered cleaner because it produces fewer harmful emissions and pollutants when burned compared to petrol or diesel, thus causing less air pollution.

items.stem: Differentiate between natural resources and human-made resources with one example each.
items.answer: Natural resources are provided by nature (e.g., air, water). Human-made resources are created by humans for their convenience (e.g., electric bulbs, furniture).

items.stem: Explain what renewable resources are, giving two examples.
items.answer: Renewable resources are those that can be renewed, replenished, or restored by natural processes within a reasonable time. Examples include air, water, and forests.

items.stem: Explain what non-renewable resources are, giving two examples.
items.answer: Non-renewable resources exist in limited quantities and are not replenished within a reasonable human time scale once used up. Examples include coal, petroleum, and minerals.

items.stem: Why is it important to conserve fossil fuels?
items.answer: Fossil fuels are limited (non-renewable) and take millions of years to form. Conserving them ensures they last longer and reduces pollution from their combustion.

items.stem: Mention two ways to reduce water wastage in daily activities.
items.answer: Turn off taps when not in use (e.g., while brushing teeth). Fix any water leakages promptly in pipes or taps.

items.stem: What are the consequences of large-scale cutting of trees on forests?
items.answer: Large-scale cutting of trees (deforestation) leads to loss of habitat for wildlife, soil erosion, and reduced capacity of forests to regenerate quickly.

items.stem: Name two ways solar energy is directly used, apart from generating electricity with solar panels.
items.answer: Solar energy is directly used for cooking in a solar cooker and for heating water in a solar water heater.

items.stem: How does throwing trash into rivers and lakes affect freshwater sources?
items.answer: Throwing trash into rivers and lakes pollutes these freshwater sources, making the water unfit for consumption by living beings and harming aquatic life.

items.stem: Describe the composition of air. Why is oxygen particularly important for most living beings?
items.answer: Air is a mixture of gases, primarily nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%). It also contains small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, and other gases. Oxygen is vital as most living beings need it for respiration, a process that releases energy from food for survival and bodily functions.

items.stem: What is rainwater harvesting? Explain its importance and describe one traditional method of rainwater harvesting practiced in India, like step wells.
items.answer: Rainwater harvesting is the collection and storage of rainwater for future use. It’s important for conserving water, especially in areas with water scarcity. Step wells (Bawadis/Vavs) are traditional structures with steps leading down to a water source. They collect rainwater and also water seeping from nearby sources, storing it for community use.

items.stem: Explain how the Sun is the primary source of energy for almost all life on Earth, tracing the energy flow from the Sun to a human eating a plant-based meal.
items.answer: The Sun emits light and heat. Plants use sunlight for photosynthesis to produce food (energy). Humans eat these plants (or animals that ate plants), thus obtaining energy that originated from the Sun. This makes the Sun the primary energy source, driving food chains and sustaining life.

items.stem: What are forests, and why are they considered a valuable natural treasure? Discuss at least three important roles of forests.
items.answer: Forests are large areas with dense plant growth. They are valuable because :

items.stem: What are rocks and minerals? Give examples of how they are utilized by humans and why their conservation is important.
items.answer: Rocks are natural solid formations, often made of minerals. Minerals are naturally occurring substances with specific compositions. Humans use rocks for construction (granite, marble) and minerals for extracting metals (iron, gold), manufacturing electronics, etc. Conservation is vital as they are non-renewable and take millions of years to form.

items.stem: What are fossil fuels? Describe how they are formed and name two common fossil fuels with one major use for each. Why is their over-dependence a concern?
items.answer: Fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas) formed from the remains of ancient organisms buried under heat and pressure over millions of years. Petroleum yields petrol (for vehicles) and natural gas is used for cooking. Over-dependence is a concern because they are non-renewable and their combustion causes significant air pollution.

items.stem: Differentiate clearly between renewable and non-renewable natural resources, providing two examples for each category. Why is the judicious use of all natural resources important?
items.answer: Renewable resources (e.g., sunlight, air, forests if managed well) can be replenished naturally within a reasonable time. Non-renewable resources (e.g., coal, petroleum, minerals) are finite and take millions of years to form. Judicious use is vital to ensure availability for future generations and to minimize environmental harm.

items.stem: Discuss two major human activities that lead to water pollution. What are the consequences of consuming polluted water?
items.answer: 1. Dumping untreated domestic sewage and industrial waste into water bodies.

items.stem: How can individual actions contribute to the conservation of fossil fuels? Suggest three practical ways an individual can reduce their fossil fuel consumption.
items.answer: Individuals can conserve fossil fuels by :

items.stem: Ajji mentions that the soil in her village is very fertile. What factors contribute to soil fertility, and how do forests play a role in maintaining it?
items.answer: Soil fertility depends on the presence of nutrients, organic matter, and a good structure that allows water retention and aeration. Forests contribute by :

items.stem: A village community relies heavily on a nearby river for drinking water, irrigation, and domestic use. Recently, a small factory set up upstream started releasing its waste directly into the river. The villagers have noticed the water becoming discolored and fish dying. (i) What natural resource is being affected in this scenario? (ii) What is the primary cause of the problem faced by the villagers? (iii) Suggest one immediate action the villagers could take and one long-term solution to address this issue.
items.answer: (i) The natural resource being affected is freshwater from the river. (ii) The primary cause is water pollution due to the factory releasing its waste into the river. (iii) Immediate action : Report the pollution to local authorities. Long-term solution : Advocate for proper waste treatment by the factory before discharge.

items.stem: Surya’s family decides to install solar panels on their rooftop. They also started using a solar cooker for some of their cooking needs and replaced their old car with an electric vehicle. (i) What natural resource are they primarily utilizing by installing solar panels and using a solar cooker? (ii) How do these actions help in conserving non- renewable resources like fossil fuels? (iii) Is solar energy a renewable or non-renewable resource? Explain why.
items.answer: (i) They are primarily utilizing energy from the Sun (solar energy). (ii) Using solar energy for electricity and cooking, and using an electric vehicle reduces the direct consumption of fossil fuels (like coal for electricity, LPG for cooking, petrol for cars). (iii) Solar energy is a renewable resource because the Sun provides a virtually inexhaustible supply of energy daily, which is naturally replenished.

items.stem: A community living near a forest extensively cuts down trees for firewood and to clear land for agriculture. Over time, they observe increased soil erosion during rains and a decrease in the local wildlife population. (i) What natural resource is being depleted due to the community’s actions? (ii) Explain how cutting down trees leads to increased soil erosion. (iii) What impact does deforestation have on local wildlife mentioned in the scenario?
items.answer: (i) Forests are the natural resource being depleted. (ii) Tree roots bind the soil together. When trees are cut, the soil becomes loose and is easily washed or blown away by rain and wind, leading to erosion. (iii) Deforestation leads to loss of habitat (shelter) and food sources for local wildlife, causing a decrease in their population.

items.stem: In a region with seasonal rainfall, a school decides to implement a rainwater harvesting system. They plan to collect rainwater from the school rooftop and store it in an underground tank for later use in toilets and gardening. (i) What is the primary purpose of this rainwater harvesting system? (ii) Is rainwater a renewable or non-renewable resource in this context? (iii) How does this initiative help the environment and the school?
items.answer: (i) The primary purpose is to conserve water by collecting and storing rainwater for non- potable uses, reducing reliance on other freshwater sources. (ii) Rainwater is a renewable resource as it is replenished through the natural water cycle. (iii) It helps the environment by reducing storm water runoff and conserving groundwater. It helps the school by providing a supplementary water source and reducing water bills.

items.stem: A farmer uses a diesel-powered tractor for ploughing his fields and a diesel pump for irrigation. He notices the price of diesel increasing and is concerned about air pollution in his village. (i) What type of natural resource is diesel? (ii) Name two negative impacts associated with the extensive use of diesel as mentioned. (iii) Suggest one alternative energy source or practice the farmer could explore for either ploughing or irrigation to reduce reliance on diesel.
items.answer: (i) Diesel is derived from petroleum, which is a non-renewable fossil fuel. (ii) Increasing price (economic impact due to resource depletion) and air pollution are two negative impacts. (iii) For irrigation, the farmer could explore solar-powered water pumps. For ploughing, traditional methods with animals or improved manual tools might be options in some contexts.
